match.reason: No bank point teaches reading a text through a particular perspective such as gender, class or culture at Stage 5 depth: the closest, Critical lenses, is Year 12 theory, and Extending interpretations covers interpretation in general rather than lens-based reading.

draft.title: Reading through a lens
card: A lens is a particular perspective a reader uses to look at a text, such as gender, class or culture. It is like choosing which pair of glasses to wear.
A lens brings some ideas forward. A class lens asks about money, work and power. A gender lens asks how male and female characters are shown and treated.
A reading through a lens must be supported with evidence from the text, such as what characters do and say, or the way a setting is described.
Different lenses can give different readings of the same text. Each can be valid if the evidence supports it.
draft.remember: A lens is a chosen perspective that brings some ideas forward, and any reading through it needs evidence from the text.

a.q: A student reads a story about a rich landowner and his farm workers by asking who holds power and who does the labour. Which lens is the student using?
opts: A class lens
A gender lens
A cultural lens
A historical lens
a.why: The student is looking at wealth, work and power, which are the focus of a class lens. A cultural lens would look at the beliefs and traditions of a group, which is not the question being asked here.
a.clue: Think about what money, work and power point to.

b.q: Two students read the same novel. Ravi reads it through a gender lens. Lena reads it through a class lens. Both give quotes and scenes from the novel to back up their ideas. What is the best conclusion?
opts: Both readings can be valid, as each is supported by evidence
Only Ravi is right, because gender is the main lens
Neither reading is valid, because the lenses differ
Only one reading is valid, because a text has one meaning
b.why: Different lenses bring different ideas forward, and each reading is sound when the text supports it. The option saying a text has one meaning is tempting, but a lens lets a reader find different ideas in the same text, as long as there is evidence.
b.clue: What makes a reading through a lens sound?

b.best: Both readings can be valid, as each is supported by evidence

problems.detail: The right option is the only hedged one ('can be valid'). The three distractors are all absolute ('Only', 'Neither', 'Only one'), so a student could pick it by elimination without knowing the idea.
